title: Mus'ab ibn Umayr
hook: a rich, perfumed youth who gave everything up and died at Uhud with a shroud too short

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ammar ibn Yasir, forced under torture to say words against his faith, and told that what counted was his heart. Your line was: the heart held. Did you go easier on yourself for one weak moment? Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

A man who is fasting is brought his food at the end of the day, and he cannot eat it. Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf, a companion who had become wealthy, sits looking at the meal and starts to remember a friend. Mus'ab ibn Umayr was killed, he says, and he was better than me. All we had to wrap him in was one cloak. If we covered his head, his feet showed. If we covered his feet, his head showed. Then he says the hard thing: now the world has been spread out for us, and I am afraid our good deeds were paid back early. And he weeps, and leaves the food where it is. Today: the young man in the short cloak.
screen: `A MEAL HE CANNOT EAT.` → `ONE CLOAK FOR A FRIEND.` → `WERE WE PAID BACK EARLY?`

segments.voice: The biographers remember Mus'ab as a young man from a comfortable Meccan family, well dressed and well perfumed, the kind people noticed in the street. Tradition says his mother cut him off when he became Muslim. A report in Tirmidhi tells of a day he walked in wearing a cloak patched with leather, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, wept, remembering how he used to live. Later, tradition says, the Prophet sent him ahead to Medina. Sahih al-Bukhari records the people of Medina saying that Mus'ab came to them with another companion, teaching them the Qur'an, before the Prophet himself arrived. So the young man who had everything became a teacher in a city that was not his own. Then Uhud. Mus'ab was killed in that battle. And here a second companion, Khabbab, tells what happened next, also in Bukhari. Some of us, Khabbab says, died before taking any of their reward in this world, and Mus'ab was one of them. He left nothing but a striped woolen cloak. When they covered his head, his feet were bare. When they covered his feet, his head was bare. So the Prophet told them: cover his head, and lay some sweet-smelling grass, idhkhir, over his feet. Hold those two pictures side by side. A youth known for his perfume, and a body covered at the feet with wild grass. Khabbab sets him against those who lived on and saw their fruit ripen. Mus'ab never saw it ripen. And Abdur-Rahman, years later, at a full table, could not eat for thinking about him. The short cloak became a measure. Not a judgment on wealth, since Abdur-Rahman was wealthy too and is honored, but a question he kept asking himself: what was given up, and what was kept back?
screen: `THE WELL-PERFUMED YOUNG MAN.` · `A TEACHER SENT TO MEDINA.` · `KILLED AT UHUD WITH ONE CLOAK.` · `GRASS LAID OVER HIS FEET.` · then, large: `THE SHROUD WAS TOO SHORT.`

segments.voice: The practice: give up one luxury. Settle, and breathe. Run through the small comforts in your day. The extra coffee, the scrolling before sleep, the second dessert, the thing in your cart you don't need. Choose one, just for today. Not as a punishment. As a way of noticing how much you are carrying. Breathe in, and picture it set down. Breathe out, and picture the space it leaves. If you pray, you can give thanks for what you have and ask for a heart that holds it lightly. The bell holds the time.
Mus'ab ibn Umayr. The young man who left comfort behind, taught the Qur'an in Medina, and was buried at Uhud in a cloak that could not cover him. Today's word.
Your line: the shroud was too short. Today, set down one luxury, and notice what you reach for in its place. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Mus'ab ibn Umayr, from the hadith of Khabbab and of Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf in Sahih al-Bukhari, as a reminder of what the early believers gave up.

fork.setup: Mus'ab has been killed at Uhud. there is one striped cloak. cover his head and his feet show; cover his feet and his head shows. what do you do?
options: cover his head, and lay grass over his feet.
cut the cloak to cover both.
fork.reveal: Khabbab says the Prophet told them to cover his head and put idhkhir grass over his feet. the young man once known for perfume was buried under wild grass.

original.note: Arabic: a striped woolen cloak, the word Khabbab uses for all Mus'ab left behind.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad detail about a funeral.
what it means: a young man who gave up comfort left nothing but one short cloak, and his friends measured their own lives against it.
what a scholar hears: Khabbab's hadith in Bukhari places Mus'ab among those who died before taking any reward in this world.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1276 (Khabbab: Mus'ab killed at Uhud, the short namirah, grass over his feet)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1274 (Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf, fasting, remembers Mus'ab's shroud and weeps)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3925 (Mus'ab comes to Medina teaching the Qur'an)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2476 (Mus'ab in a patched cloak; the Prophet weeps remembering his former life)

notes: Audit: hook said he wept 'until the food goes cold'; Bukhari 1274 says he wept and left the food, so the line now says that. 'Then he was sent away from Mecca' (could read as exile) changed to 'the Prophet sent him ahead to Medina', framed as tradition.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm all four.
The perfume, fine clothes and his mother cutting him off come from the sira (e.g. Ibn Sa'd), so they are framed as 'the biographers remember' and 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Bukhari 3925 says Mus'ab and Ibn Umm Maktum were the first to come; 'first' was left out to keep the line simple. Ibn Umm Maktum is not named.
Bukhari 1274 uses burdah for the cloak; 1276 (Khabbab) uses namirah. The original game uses namirah; confirm transliteration and stress.
Abdur-Rahman's words are paraphrased; confirm the paraphrase of 'our good deeds were paid back early'.
